'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Vermont|Governor]] | before_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsVT}} The '''2014 Vermont gubernatorial election''' took place on November 4, 2014, to elect the [[List of governors of Vermont|governor of Vermont]], concurrently with [[2014 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Peter Shumlin]] ran for reelection to a third term in office against [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Scott Milne]], [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] businessman Dan Feliciano and several other minor party and independent candidates. Based on election polling, Shumlin's large financial advantage and the state's [[Red states and blue states|strong Democratic lean in presidential elections]], Shumlin was expected to win easily, but he received only a [[Plurality (voting)|plurality]], not a [[majority]], of the vote and polled only 2,434 votes more than Milne out of 193,087 cast. The [[Constitution of Vermont]] requires that the 180-member [[Vermont General Assembly]] choose the winner when no candidate receives over 50% of the popular vote.{{cite news|title=Close election recalls recent recounts|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/06/election-recalls-recent-recounts/18622085/|access-date=November 11, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|date=November 7, 2014}} As a result, on January 8, 2015,{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/12/08/video-scott-milne-asks-lawmakers-vote-january/|title=Trail Mix: Milne concedes he won't concede|work=VTDigger|author=Anne Galloway|date=December 8, 2014|access-date=January 4, 2015}} the Assembly chose Shumlin over Milne by a vote of 110 to 69, with one abstention.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/01/08/vermont-legislature-vote/21394309/|title=Shumlin defeats Milne in Legislature governor vote|author=Free Press Staff|date=January 8, 2015|access-date=January 8, 2015}} The result of the election prompted much debate and analysis amongst commentators and the political parties. The [[2014 United States elections|2014 U.S. elections]] saw Republicans make sweeping gains in federal, state, and local offices across the country, and Republicans won gubernatorial victories in the Democratic-leaning Northeastern states of [[2014 Maryland gubernatorial election|Maryland]] and [[2014 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|Massachusetts]]. With a margin of 1.3%, this election was the second-closest race of the [[2014 United States gubernatorial elections|2014 gubernatorial election cycle]], behind only [[2014 Florida gubernatorial election|the election in Florida]]. {{As of|2026}}, this was also the last time a Democrat won the governorship of Vermont. ==Background== Four-term Republican governor [[Jim Douglas]] did not run for reelection [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2010]]. In the race to succeed him, Democratic nominee [[Peter Shumlin]], the [[President pro tempore of the Vermont State Senate|president pro tempore]] of the [[Vermont Senate]], received 49.5% of the vote while Republican nominee [[List of lieutenant governors of Vermont|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Brian Dubie]] received 47.7%. As neither candidate received a majority, the General Assembly was required to pick the winner in January 2011. Dubie did not contest the vote; he conceded the race on election night and called for Vermont to "unite" around Shumlin.{{cite web |url=http://www.vpr.net/news_detail/89189/dubie-asks-vermonters-to-unite-around-new-governor/ |title=Dubie Asks Vermonters To Unite Around New Governor |work=Vermont Public Radio |date=November 3, 2010 |access-date=August 3, 2013}} Shumlin won the Assembly vote 145 to 28, with seven legislators not voting.{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/article/20101103/NEWS02/101103024/1007/news02/Dubie-concedes-to-Shumlin-in-Vermont-governor-a-race|title=Dubie concedes to Shumlin in Vermont governor race|publisher=burlingtonfreepress.com|date=2010-11-03}}{{Dead link|date=July 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}Vermont General Assembly, [http://www.leg.state.vt.us/docs/2012/journal/ja110106.pdf Journal of the Joint Assembly], January 6, 2011, page 5 Shumlin was reelected [[2012 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2012]] against Republican state senator and former [[Vermont Auditor of Accounts]] [[Randy Brock]] by a landslide, 57.8% to 37.6%.{{cite web|url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=726426|title=VT Governor 2014|publisher=Our Campaigns|access-date=February 28, 2016}} Vermont and [[New Hampshire]] are the only states in the country whose governors are elected every two years. Former governor Douglas and [[List of lieutenant governors of Vermont|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Phil Scott]] announced early on that they would not run, and it was not until March 2014 that a candidate entered the race: marijuana legalization activist and former Independent gubernatorial candidate Emily Peyton.{{cite web|url=http://blogs.burlingtonfreepress.com/politics/2014/03/07/theres-a-candidate-running-for-governor-as-a-republican-but-isnt-really-from-the-party/|title=There's a candidate running for governor as a Republican — but isn't really from the party|date=March 7, 2014|access-date=March 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Nancy Remsen}} This spurred Republicans to recruit a serious candidate, but they struggled to do so. Former [[Wall Street]] banker Bruce Lisman announced in May 2014 that he was not running, and attention turned to former state senator and 2012 nominee [[Randy Brock]], State Representative [[Heidi Scheuermann]] and businessman [[Scott Milne]].{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2014/05/12/republican-milne-considers-run-governor/9009379/|title=Republican Milne considers run for governor|date=May 12, 2014|access-date=May 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Terri Hallenbeck}} In May, Scheuermann said that she would not run, leaving the party with a month until the June 12 filing deadline to find a candidate.{{cite web|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2014/05/13/scheuermann-opts-run-governor/9032953/|title=Scheuermann opts against run for governor|date=May 13, 2014|access-date=May 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|author=Terri Hallenbeck}} Milne, who was traveling in Africa, announced that he would decide shortly before the deadline. Shumlin won 112, or 40.7%, and they were tied in one other.{{cite news|last1=Heintz|first1=Paul|title=Close Call: Seven Reasons Shumlin Nearly Lost|url=http://www.sevendaysvt.com/vermont/close-call-seven-reasons-shumlin-nearly-lost/Content?oid=2472138|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=Seven Days|date=November 12, 2014}} Shumlin won the state's biggest voting area, [[Burlington, Vermont|Burlington]] (representing 9,604 gubernatorial voters), by a margin of 66% to 23%. Of the state's 10 largest municipalities, Shumlin also won [[South Burlington, Vermont|South Burlington]], [[Bennington, Vermont|Bennington]], [[Montpelier, Vermont|Montpelier]], [[Hartford, Vermont|Hartford]] and [[Middlebury, Vermont|Middlebury]]. Milne won [[Essex, Vermont|Essex]], [[Colchester, Vermont|Colchester]], [[Rutland (city), Vermont|Rutland City]], [[Williston, Vermont|Williston]] and [[Barre (town), Vermont|Barre Town]]. Of Vermont's 13 multi-member Senate districts, aligning roughly with the state's 14 counties, Milne won eight (61.5%) and Shumlin five (38.5%). Milne won the popular vote in 53 House districts; Shumlin won in 51. ==General Assembly vote== Since 1853, the General Assembly has selected the first-place finisher in every gubernatorial election that has come before it,{{cite news|url=http://www.timesargus.com/article/20141110/NEWS03/711109999 |title=Plurality or politics? |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |work=Barre Montpelier Times Argus}} most recently in [[2010 Vermont gubernatorial election|2010]], when Shumlin received 49.5% of the vote and was chosen over Republican Brian Dubie, and in [[2002 Vermont gubernatorial election|2002]], when the Democratic-controlled legislature picked Republican [[Jim Douglas]], who had received 44.9%, over Democrat [[Doug Racine]], who received 42.4%.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/10/lawmakers-likely-stick-secret-ballot/ |title=Lawmakers likely to stick with secret ballot |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |work=VT Digger}} The Assembly most recently reversed a plurality vote in the 1976 lieutenant gubernatorial election, when the Republican-controlled legislature picked Republican [[T. Garry Buckley]] rather than Democrat John Alden, who was suspected, and later convicted, of insurance fraud.{{cite news|title=Close election recalls recent recounts|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/06/election-recalls-recent-recounts/18622085/|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=The Burlington Free Press|date=November 7, 2014}}{{cite news|title=T. Garry Buckley|url=http://www.timesargus.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20120527/FEATURES15/705279943/1014/OPINION06|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=Barre Montpelier Times Argus|date=May 27, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113162135/http://www.timesargus.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20120527%2FFEATURES15%2F705279943%2F1014%2FOPINION06|archive-date=November 13, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}{{cite news|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/wait-legislature-choosing-governor|title=Wait, The Legislature Is Choosing The Governor?|access-date=November 13, 2014|publisher=Vermont Public Radio|date=November 6, 2014}} Although the second-place finisher usually concedes the race, as happened in 2002 and 2010,{{cite news|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/11/06/elec02.governor/index.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141113155328/http://edition.cnn.com/2002/ALLPOLITICS/11/06/elec02.governor/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 13, 2014|title=Two candidates claim Alabama gubernatorial race|date=November 7, 2002|access-date=November 13, 2014|publisher=CNN}}{{cite news|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2010/11/03/vermont-election-results-_2_n_773154.html|title=Vermont Election Results: Brian Dubie Concedes To Peter Shumlin In 2010 Governor's Race|date=November 3, 2010|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=The Huffington Post}} Milne refused to concede. He considered requesting a recount, but did not do so, reasoning that it was "extremely unlikely, almost unfathomable, that a recount would put either candidate above the 50 percent mark."{{cite news|url=http://wamc.org/post/milne-wont-seek-recount-may-ask-legislators-elect-him-governor|title=Milne Won't Seek Recount, But May Ask Legislators To Elect Him Governor|access-date=November 14, 2014|publisher=WAMC|date=November 13, 2014|archive-date=November 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129021839/http://wamc.org/post/milne-wont-seek-recount-may-ask-legislators-elect-him-governor|url-status=dead}} Before the election, Milne said that if Shumlin won a plurality, he would support him and would expect Shumlin to do the same if the situation were reversed. After the election, however, he said, "it's clear that 54% of Vermonters want a new governor, and a new path forward."{{cite news|url=http://www.rutlandherald.com/article/20141106/THISJUSTIN/141109966|title=Milne Calls Shumlin's Claim of Victory Premature|access-date=November 7, 2014|work=Rutland Herald|date=November 6, 2014}} As 91 votes are needed to elect the governor from the 180-member body and Democrats and Progressives held 112 seats, it was considered unlikely that Milne would win.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/12/scott-milne-pursuit-governorship/ |title=Margolis: Scott Milne and the pursuit of the governorship |work=VT Digger |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=November 23, 2014}} Milne argued that legislators should decide the election in line with how their individual districts voted.{{cite news|author=Laura Krantz|title=Milne exploring all options|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/06/milne-exploring-options/|access-date=November 13, 2014|work=VTDigger|date=November 6, 2014}} Neal Goswami of the Vermont Press Bureau calculated that if each legislator voted according to the results in their district, the vote would result in a 90–90 tie. Milne disagreed with this calculation and claimed voting according to district outcome would result in his winning 93–87. {{quote box |width = 29em |border = 1px |align = right |halign = left |quote = ''The fact is that fewer people voted for Scott Milne than voted for Peter Shumlin. Milne did not get a majority, either. I just don't think he has a case to be made that a majority, or even a plurality of voters, want him to be governor. I don't think that I will probably have to persuade [other legislators of this], quite frankly.'' |source = [[Speaker of the Vermont House of Representatives|State House Speaker]] [[Shap Smith]], whose district voted for Milne, explaining why he would vote for Shumlin }} Republican legislative leaders said that they would not [[Whip (politics)|whip]] their members to vote for Shumlin, leaving them free to vote their consciences. Though Republican [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|lieutenant governor]] [[Phil Scott]] did not have a vote, he said that he would vote for Shumlin, and Republican state representative [[Kurt Wright]] said that he would do so.{{cite news |url=http://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/ci_26895237/vermont-gop-says-party-will-follow-conscience-governor |title=Vermont: GOP says party will follow conscience on governor vote |work=The Berkshire Eagle |date=November 8, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-date=November 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141112001928/http://www.berkshireeagle.com/news/ci_26895237/vermont-gop-says-party-will-follow-conscience-governor |url-status=dead }} Initially, no Democrats indicated that they would vote for Milne. Indeed, several Democrats whose districts voted for Milne over Shumlin said that they would vote for Shumlin, citing his plurality win. Public Radio |author=Bob Kinzel |date=November 10, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} [[File:Jim Douglas-2009.jpg|left|thumb|225px|Former Republican Governor Jim Douglas, who urged Milne not to campaign for votes in the General Assembly]] On December 8, Milne held a press conference in which he defied suggestions that he would concede by officially announcing that he was asking state legislators to vote for him. He went on to say that he would not be "pro-actively" trying to convince legislators to vote for him, nor would he start "twisting arms", but that his "door is open" and called on legislators to "consider the record of the incumbent" and what was "best" for Vermont.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/12/08/milne-announces-plan-seek-election/20088821/ |title=Milne continues push for governor's office |work=Burlington Free Press |author=April Burbank |date=December 8, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.montpelierbridge.com/2014/12/scott-milne-up-close-and-personal-qa/ |title=Scott Milne: Up Close and Personal Q&A |work=The Bridge |date=December 19, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} Shumlin responded that he was "honored to have received the most votes in this election and would not want to serve as governor if I did not." He went on to say that he believed that "the Legislature will honor the long democratic tradition of electing the candidate who received the most votes." After Milne's announcement, Independent State Representative Paul Poirier, a liberal whose district voted for Milne by a 2-to-1 margin, announced that he would vote for Milne. One Democrat, State Representative Jim Condon, said that he would vote for Milne, also citing his district's support for Milne over Shumlin. Political science professors Eric Davis and Garrison Nelson and House Minority Leader Don Turner expected the General Assembly vote to roughly follow party lines, with Milne receiving about one-third of the votes, including most of the Republicans and a few Democrats and Independents. On December 17, Shumlin announced that he was dropping his plan to implement single-payer healthcare. The reforms, which required business and personal tax increases, had never advanced beyond the framework stage. Shumlin, who had missed two earlier financing deadlines, said that "this is not the right time" because the federal government had offered less funding than expected and "the potential economic disruption and risks would be too great to small businesses, working families and the state's economy."{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2014/12/vermont-peter-shumlin-single-payer-health-care-113653.html |title=Vermont bails on single-payer health care |work=Politico |author=Sarah Wheaton |date=December 17, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} The media also cited controversy surrounding comments made by economist [[Jonathan Gruber (economist)|Jonathan Gruber]], who was involved in $30,000 to air television advertisements aimed at pressuring legislators to vote for Milne. The group's founder, retired [[United States Navy]] Captain Bill Round, said that legislators should vote against Shumlin because "he's promised a lot and failed to deliver."{{cite news|url=https://vtdigger.org/2014/12/30/group-launches-ad-grassroots-effort-pressure-lawmakers-vote-milne/ |title=Group launches ad, grassroots effort to pressure lawmakers to vote for Milne |work=VTDigger |author=Anne Galloway |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}}{{cite news |url=http://wamc.org/post/group-running-ads-urging-legislature-vote-milne-governor |title=Group Running Ads Urging Legislature To Vote For Milne For Governor |publisher=Vermont Public Radio |author=Pat Bradley |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014 |archive-date=January 4, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104181711/http://wamc.org/post/group-running-ads-urging-legislature-vote-milne-governor |url-status=dead }} Round did not reveal the source of the group's funding. Milne said that while he had no connection to the group, he appreciated the sentiment.{{cite news|url=http://digital.vpr.net/post/group-runs-ad-calling-election-scott-milne |title=Group Runs Ad Calling For Election Of Scott Milne |publisher=Vermont Public Radio |author=Peter Hirschfeld |date=December 30, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} By contrast, Shumlin said that he would "absolutely not" run any advertisements, nor would he campaign for legislators' votes or spend any money. He added that he was "not worried" about the vote.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/12/30/shumlin-says-worried-vote/21056955/ |title=Shumlin says he's not worried about vote |publisher=Burlington Free Press |author=Peter Hirschfeld |date=December 31, 2014 |access-date=January 6, 2014}} In early January, Milne reiterated that he was not actively campaigning for legislators' votes but said that he felt that his odds of victory were "getting better on a weekly basis, if not a daily basis."{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/local/2015/01/03/milne-says-odds-improving/21231247/ |title=Milne says his odds improving |work=Burlington Free Press |author=Dave Gram |date=January 3, 2014 |access-date=January 4, 2014}} Shumlin said that if Milne were to win, Vermont would be "paralyzed", as the new administration lacked the time needed to assemble a new staff and draft a budget for the 2016 fiscal year. He also offered his support for amending the state constitution so that as long as a plurality winner received at least 40% of the vote, the Assembly would not be required to decide the election.{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2015/01/05/milne-shumlin-vermont-governor-legislature/21300367/ |title=Lawmakers to decide gubernatorial election Thursday |work=Burlington Free Press |author=Dave Gram |date=January 6, 2014 |access-date=January 8, 2014}} On January 8, the General Assembly voted to reelect Shumlin by 110 votes to 69, with one legislator not voting. Shumlin stated that he was "grateful for the opportunity to continue serving this state I love. I expect this will be a productive session addressing the issues Vermonters care about so deeply." Milne said that it was "a good day for Vermont ... I was happy to be a part of it. I think the road that's led us here has a lot of people feeling like one person can make a difference." Milne did not rule out running again [[2016 Vermont gubernatorial election|in 2016]], although he later declined and instead [[2016 United States Senate election in Vermont|ran for the United States Senate]], losing to incumbent [[Patrick Leahy]] by almost 30 points.{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2015/01/peter-shumlin-scott-milne-vermont-governor-race-114051.html |title=Vermont legislature to pick next governor Thursday |work=Politico |author=Kyle Cheney |date=January 7, 2014 |access-date=January 8, 2014}} ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = 2014 Vermont gubernatorial election, Vermont General Assembly vote}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | party = Democratic Party (United States) | candidate = [[Peter Shumlin]] (incumbent) | votes = 110 | percentage = 61.45% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | party = Republican Party (United States) | candidate = [[Scott Milne]] | votes = 69 | percentage = 38.55% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Libertarian Party (United States) |candidate = Dan Feliciano |votes = 0 |percentage = 0.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 179 of 180 | percentage = 100.00% | change = }} {{Election box hold with party link without swing |winner = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Election box end}} ==Analysis== As no candidate received a majority of the vote, the [[Vermont General Assembly]] was required to decide the election, choosing among the top three vote-getters, Shumlin, Milne and Feliciano. The result came as a surprise to most observers, who had expected Shumlin to win easily.{{cite news|url=http://www.wptz.com/news/vermont-new-york/burlington/people-react-to-vermont-governors-race/29571318 |title=People react to Vermont governor's race |publisher=WPTZ |date=November 5, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.stowetoday.com/stowe_reporter/news/article_46a6096a-653b-11e4-a88b-f3f03141b952.html |title=Milne nearly topples Shumlin |work=Stowe Reporter |date=November 5, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}}{{cite news|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2014/11/13/what-the-hell-happened-in-vermont.html |title=What the Hell Happened in Vermont?! |work=The Daily Beast |date=November 13, 2014 |access-date=November 13, 2014}} [[RealClearPolitics]] rated the race "Likely Democratic" and ''[[The Cook Political Report]]'', ''[[Daily Kos|Daily Kos Elections]]'', ''[[Governing (magazine)|Governing]]'', ''[[Stuart Rothenberg|The Rothenberg Political Report]]'' and ''[[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]'' all rated the race "Safe Democratic".[[2014 United States gubernatorial elections#Safe seats]] RealClearPolitics reported an average lead in the polls of 15.2% for Shumlin{{cite news|url=http://www.realclearpolitics.com/epolls/2014/governor/vt/vermont_governor_milne_vs_shumlin-5207.html |title=Vermont Governor - Milne vs. Shumlin |work=RealClearPolitics |access-date=November 11, 2014}} and HuffPost Pollster's model estimated Shumlin would beat Milne 51.1% to 37% with the probability that Shumlin would win the election at 95%.{{cite news |url=http://elections.huffingtonpost.com/pollster/2014-vermont-governor-milne-vs-shumlin |title=2014 Vermont Governor: Milne vs. Shumlin |work=elections.huffingtonpost.com |date=October 27, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-date=November 11, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141111192510/http://elections.huffingtonpost.com/pollster/2014-vermont-governor-milne-vs-shumlin |url-status=dead }} [[File:Leahy2009.jpg|right|thumb|225px|Democratic U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy, whose support Shumlin touted]] Analyzing the results, ''[[The Burlington Free Press]]'' pointed to Shumlin's relatively soft numbers in opinion polls – he was in the mid-40s in the last four polls of the race – as evidence that voters were dissatisfied with the progress the state had made in instituting [[Vermont health care reform|single-payer health care]], with rising property taxes, and with the unsuccessful roll-out of [[Vermont Health Connect]], the state's [[Health insurance marketplace|federal health care exchange]].{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/05/two-term-incumbent-governor-nearly-lost/18563053/ |title=How a two-term incumbent governor nearly lost |work=The Burlington Free Press |date=November 6, 2014 |access-date=November 11, 2014}} Shumlin's internal polls showed a close race and he touted an endorsement from U.S. senator [[Patrick Leahy]] to try to put him over 50%. By comparison, Milne lagged in fundraising and spending, with $100,000 available compared to Shumlin's $1.1 million, which meant that he could not afford to pay for polling. Opinions varied about the effect Libertarian nominee Dan Feliciano's candidacy had on the result. Former governor [[Jim Douglas|Douglas]] suggested that Feliciano split the anti-Shumlin vote. ''The Burlington Free Press'' speculated that Feliciano drew voters dissatisfied with Shumlin but who would have voted for Milne if they had realized that he had a chance to prevail. Feliciano stated that he was "not a spoiler" but drew voters who could not bring themselves to vote for the Republican candidate. A Feliciano campaign consultant felt, based on polling, that her candidate's stance against Shumlin's healthcare policy garnered votes. Milne, who did no polling, began criticizing Shumlin's healthcare policy later in the campaign than Feliciano. Republicans wondered whether they should have done more to push Feliciano out, whether Milne should have run more strongly against single-payer, whether 2012 nominee and former state auditor [[Randy Brock]] should have run again, and whether the state party should have been less focused on state legislative races. Analysis by political experts pointed to the record-low voter turnout–around 43.6%–and that 39,000 more people voted for Democratic congressman [[Peter Welch]] than voted for Shumlin as a sign of dissatisfaction with Shumlin. [[University of Vermont]] political science professor Garrison Nelson said that "the people who showed up are the angry ones" and that, unlike Shumlin, "Welch demonstrated an appeal far beyond just the Democratic base."{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/11/analysis-many-voters-stayed-home-rather-back-shumlin/ |title=Analysis: many voters stayed home rather than back Shumlin |work=VT Digger |date=November 11, 2014 |access-date=November 18, 2014}} In a news conference on November 12, Shumlin stated that the result was "humbling" and said that he would "listen, learn, reflect [and] be more inclusive." He also pledged to move ahead with single-payer health care and to address school spending, property taxes and the $100-million budget gap.{{cite news|url=http://vtdigger.org/2014/11/12/humbled-shumlin-vows-listen-learn/ |title=Shumlin committed to single-payer, vows to listen, learn |work=VT Digger |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=November 18, 2014}} On June 8, 2015, Shumlin announced that he would not run for a fourth term in [[2016 Vermont gubernatorial election|2016]]. He said that he had "never seen politics as a lifelong career" and "decided to make this decision now because I want these next 18 months to be about the work that we still have to do." He said that his decision was "not driven by poll numbers; [nor] driven by politics" and that after leaving office in January 2017, he would return to his family business in [[Putney, Vermont|Putney]].{{cite news|url=http://www.burlingtonfreepress.com/story/news/2015/06/08/shumlin-decided-against-2016-re-election/28690591/ |title=Shumlin decides against 2016 re-election bid
